title: Review: Electron-pair sharing reactions

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Curly arrow
items.clue: Shows the movement of an electron pair.

items.label: Leaving group
items.clue: Departs taking both electrons of the broken bond.

items.label: Electrophile
items.clue: Accepts a pair from its partner to form a new covalent bond.

items.label: Electrophilic addition
items.clue: The typical reaction of alkenes: a species attracted to the C=C joins across it.

questions.stem:
2-bromo-2-methylpropane reacts with water:
(CH₃)₃CBr + H₂O → (CH₃)₃COH + HBr
Which reactant acts as the nucleophile, and why?

options.text: Neither, as neither reactant carries a negative charge
(CH₃)₃CBr, as its C atom accepts a pair of electrons
H₂O, as its O atom and the C atom each give one electron
H₂O, as a lone pair on its O atom forms the new bond to carbon

questions.explanation: The O atom of water has lone pairs; one is donated to the electron-deficient carbon atom, forming the C–O bond of the alcohol. A neutral molecule can be a nucleophile.

questions.stem: 1-bromopropane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which equation represents the reaction that occurs?

options.text: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂⁻ + HOBr
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CHBr⁻ + H₂O
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH⁻ + Br

questions.explanation: OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon bonded to Br, and the C–Br bonding pair leaves with Br as the bromide ion. The product is propan-1-ol.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the heterolytic fission of a covalent bond?

options.text: One bonding electron goes to each fragment, so radicals form.
Both bonding electrons go to one fragment, so two ions form.
Both bonding electrons go to one fragment, which becomes positive.
It is the breaking of a bond that joins two different elements.

questions.explanation: In heterolytic fission one fragment keeps the bonding pair and becomes an anion; the other becomes a cation, e.g. H–Br → H⁺ + Br⁻.

questions.stem:
Ethene reacts with bromine:
CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br
Which reactant acts as the electrophile?

options.text: Br₂, as it accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond
Ethene, as its C=C bond is rich in electrons
Neither, as neither reactant carries a positive charge
Ethene, as its C atoms need electrons for an octet

questions.explanation: Br₂ accepts the electron pair donated by the electron-rich C=C bond, forming a C–Br bond. A neutral molecule can be an electrophile.

questions.stem: Ethene is bubbled through a solution of bromine in an organic solvent at room temperature, in the dark. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂BrCH₂Br forms by addition.
The bromine loses its colour as CH₂=CHBr forms by substitution.
No reaction occurs, as Br₂ has no positive charge.
No reaction occurs, as UV light is needed to split Br₂.

questions.explanation: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.

questions.stem: Which statement describes how a nucleophile forms a new bond to its reaction partner?

options.text: It donates both electrons of the new covalent bond.
It accepts the two electrons of the new covalent bond.
It gives one electron, and its partner gives the other.
It transfers electrons, forming an ionic bond.

questions.explanation: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor: it supplies both electrons of the new bond, usually from a lone pair, and the electrophile supplies none.

questions.stem: In the reaction CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻ a new C–O bond forms. Where do the two electrons of the new C–O bond come from?

options.text: One from the O atom and one from the C atom
Both from the C–Br bond, which becomes the new C–O bond
Both from a lone pair on the O atom of the OH⁻ ion
Both from the C atom, which donates them to the O

questions.explanation: OH⁻ is the nucleophile: a lone pair on its oxygen is donated to the δ+ carbon and becomes the C–O bonding pair. The C–Br pair leaves with Br⁻.

questions.stem: Hydrogen chloride undergoes heterolytic fission to form H⁺ and Cl⁻. Which describes the curly arrow for this change?

options.text: It starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on the H atom.
It starts on the Cl atom and points back to the H–Cl bond.
It starts on the H atom and shows the H⁺ ion moving away.
It starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on the Cl atom.

questions.explanation: A curly arrow shows an electron pair moving from its source to its destination. The H–Cl bonding pair moves onto Cl, which becomes Cl⁻, leaving H⁺.

questions.stem:
Ammonia reacts with hydrogen ions:
NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺
Which species acts as the electrophile?

options.text: NH₃, as its nitrogen atom carries a lone pair of electrons
Neither, as N and H each supply one electron to the bond
H⁺, as it accepts the lone pair on the nitrogen atom
H⁺, as it forms an ionic bond with the nitrogen atom of NH₃

questions.explanation: H⁺ has no electrons and accepts the lone pair of nitrogen to form the new N–H bond. A positively charged species that accepts a pair is an electrophile.

questions.stem: Ethene is mixed with hydrogen bromide gas at room temperature. Which statement is correct?

options.text: HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₂BrCH₂Br.
A Br atom replaces one H atom, forming CH₂=CHBr.
HBr adds across the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂Br.
No reaction occurs, as the HBr molecule is neutral.

questions.explanation: H adds to one carbon and Br to the other: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br, bromoethane.

questions.stem: Why are alkenes susceptible to attack by electrophiles?

options.text: The C=C double bond is weaker than a C–C single bond.
The C=C double bond is a region of high electron density.
The carbon atoms of C=C are deficient in electrons.
The C=C carbon atoms need more electrons for an octet.

questions.explanation: The double bond concentrates electron density between and around the two carbon atoms, and this electron-rich region attracts electron-pair acceptors.

questions.stem: But-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, undergoes hydration when heated with steam in the presence of an acid catalyst. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butane-2,3-diol.
An OH group replaces an H atom, forming but-2-en-2-ol.
H atoms from water add across C=C, forming butane.
Water adds across the C=C bond, forming butan-2-ol.

questions.explanation: H adds to one carbon of C=C and OH to the other: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, butan-2-ol.

questions.stem: In the first step of the acid-catalysed addition of water to ethene, H⁺ bonds to one carbon atom of the C=C bond, forming CH₃CH₂⁺. Which species acts as the Lewis base in this step?

options.text: Neither, as ethene has no lone pair to donate
H⁺, as it accepts the electron pair of the C=C bond
Ethene, as its C=C electrons form the new C–H bond
Ethene, as it gives two electrons to H⁺ in an ionic bond

questions.explanation: The electron pair of the second bond of C=C is donated to H⁺ and becomes the new C–H bond. The electron-pair donor, ethene, is the Lewis base; H⁺ is the Lewis acid.

questions.stem: In the reaction CH₃CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + Br⁻, which statement about OH⁻ is correct?

options.text: It is a nucleophile, and so it is a Lewis acid.
It is an electrophile, as it is rich in electrons.
It is a nucleophile but no base, as it gains no H⁺.
It is a nucleophile, and so it is also a Lewis base.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the carbon atom. Every nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, so it is also a Lewis base.

questions.stem: A complex ion contains one Cr³⁺ ion, four H₂O ligands and two Cl⁻ ligands. What is the charge on the complex ion [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]?
questions.explanation: Charge = (+3) + 2(−1) + 4(0) = +1. The Cl⁻ ligands each add −1 and the neutral water ligands add nothing, so the complex is [CrCl₂(H₂O)₄]⁺.

questions.stem: A single enantiomer of 2-bromobutane, CH₃CHBrCH₂CH₃, reacts with aqueous hydroxide ions by the SN2 mechanism. Which statement about this reaction is correct?

options.text: OH⁻ takes the exact place of Br, so the configuration is retained.
A carbocation forms first, so a racemic mixture is produced.
OH⁻ attacks opposite Br, so the configuration is inverted.
A stable five-bonded intermediate forms, then Br⁻ leaves.

questions.explanation: In SN2 the nucleophile approaches the δ+ carbon from the side opposite the leaving group. As Br⁻ leaves, the other three groups flip over, so a single enantiomer of butan-2-ol forms with inverted configuration: SN2 is stereospecific.

questions.stem: Under identical conditions, which reacts faster with aqueous hydroxide ions, 1-bromobutane or 1-chlorobutane, and why?

options.text: 1-chlorobutane, as the C–Cl bond is more polar than C–Br
1-chlorobutane, as the smaller Cl atom blocks attack less
Neither; both react at the same rate, as OH⁻ attacks C
1-bromobutane, as the C–Br bond is weaker than the C–Cl bond

questions.explanation: The C–Br bond enthalpy is lower than that of C–Cl, so it breaks more easily and bromide is the better leaving group. 1-bromobutane reacts faster.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with bromine by electrophilic addition. How does the non-polar Br₂ molecule come to act as an electrophile?

options.text: Br₂ first ionizes into Br⁺ and Br⁻, and Br⁺ accepts the C=C electron pair.
UV light splits Br₂ into Br atoms, and each Br atom adds to a carbon.
One Br atom donates an electron pair to C=C, forming a C–Br bond.
The electron-rich C=C induces a dipole in Br₂, and Brδ+ accepts the C=C pair.

questions.explanation: As Br₂ approaches, the C=C electron density repels the Br–Br bonding pair, making the near Br δ+. A curly arrow from C=C to Brδ+ and one from Br–Br to Brδ− give a carbocation and Br⁻, which then bonds to it.
